problem: Existing mobile-manipulation and object-rearrangement systems need explicit goal arrangements or demonstration data. They also ignore how the robot's standing position affects both manipulation feasibility and navigation efficiency, so they handle underspecified requests like 'set the table' poorly.
motivation: Real user requests are underspecified, and a good table setting depends on common sense (fork left, knife right). LLMs hold this knowledge without needing training data. Feasible and efficient execution also requires choosing base positions under uncertainty (e.g., chairs blocking access), which motivates combining LLM goal generation with a vision-learned feasibility model.
key_idea: Use an LLM to generate symbolic and geometric tabletop goal configurations, then use GROP (an FCN feasibility heatmap trained in simulation, plus utility-based task-motion planning) to choose standing positions and plans that trade off feasibility against cost.
insight: Common-sense goal generation and visually grounded base-position selection are complementary. In simulation, GROP alone is as fast as LLM-GROP but gets much lower user ratings, while LATP and TPRA are both slower and rated lower. The LLM comparison shows no single LLM wins on all tasks: GPT-4 is best on 4 of 8 tasks, and GPT-3 is best on the 5-object Task 8.
method: Symbolic relation generation: template-based prompt (zero- or few-shot) asks the LLM for spatial relations (left of, above, etc.) among tableware; ASP rules written by experts detect contradictions and trigger re-prompting.

Geometric relation generation: a second template asks the LLM for distances in cm, coordinates are computed from a central origin object (e.g., plate), and 2D Gaussian sampling with rejection (relation consistency, no overlap, within table bounds) yields M candidate configurations.

GROP feasibility evaluator: an FCN maps a top-down image (64x32) to a heatmap of navigation+manipulation success probability. It is trained as an N-class pixel classifier on simulated trials (100 tasks, N=5 trials, 24x8 pixels, 96,000 samples), and inference takes the probability-weighted average over the classes.

Task-level feasibility and utility: Fea^t averages heatmap-weighted sampled standing positions; plan utility U(p)=R·F(p)−C(p) trades success against navigation/manipulation cost, and the highest-utility plan across task plans and object configurations is returned.

Task and motion planning: a task planner enumerates satisficing plans interleaving navigation and manipulation actions, sampled standing positions form the base motion sequence, and MoveIt handles the arm on the real robot.
Real-world deployment: object and obstacle poses are estimated to build a digital twin from the same sim assets, and top-down views are rendered as input to the FCN to sidestep the sim-to-real gap.

setting.backbone: GPT-3 text-davinci-003 (frozen, default) for goal generation; also GPT-4, Gemini-1.5-flash, Claude-3.5-sonnet; FCN feasibility evaluator trained from scratch
setting.training_data: FCN trained only on simulated Gazebo trial data (100 tasks x 5 trials x 24x8 pixels = 96,000 samples); LLMs used off-the-shelf with no training
setting.observation: top-down RGB image of the table and obstacles (rendered digital twin in real world) plus a prebuilt map with rangefinder for navigation
setting.action_space: symbolic navigation and load/unload actions between locations, with sampled 2D base poses as navigation goals; arm via MoveIt
setting.privileged: known table shapes and locations, 3D models of all objects, QR codes for object localization, and a utensil holder for grasping; chairs sensed at planning time

numbers.extra: real robot, 10 human raters, 1-5 scale; ratings shown per task in easy / chair-top / chair-bottom
numbers.evidence: Figure 6 caption: 'Successes total to 38 trials, while failure accounts to 7 trials, producing an overall 84.4% success rate'; Table 4 user ratings

numbers.eval_set_note: 8 tasks, 20 runs each; 5 raters; user ratings by LLM in Table 5
numbers.extra: 10 human raters, 1-5 scale, per task mean ± std

numbers_note: Comparison with baselines (TPRA, LATP, GROP) is shown only in figures (Figure 'main' and 'individual'), so no baseline numbers or exact LLM-GROP GPT-3 rating and time from that comparison are available. This is not a navigation benchmark paper.
results: LLM-GROP achieved an 84.4% real-robot success rate (38/45 trials), with average user ratings of about 3.1 to 3.9. In simulation it obtained the highest user rating and lowest execution time versus TPRA, LATP and GROP, and raters still scored it below experienced human waiters. Swapping the LLM shows GPT-4 reaches up to 4.98 on 3-4 object tasks but drops on the 5-object Task 8.
limitations: Feasibility model trained only on rectangular tables with widely spaced objects. Irregular tables or crowded tabletops are likely to fail.
Assumes complete 3D models of all objects, a top-down view for perception, and interleaved rather than simultaneous navigation and manipulation.
LLM outputs are inconsistent across tasks (a large drop on 5-object tasks); the paper reports no cost analysis of querying LLMs, and human ratings remain below expert waiters.
